body: Adds a bit_cast function, copied from https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/numeric/bit_cast

@clayjohn this is the shader for computing the static motion vectors.

Also, I haven't implemented MSAA support yet. I don't think that will be hard.
is it worth putting this behind a support check so platforms without metalfx won't show those options?

this condition gets repeated a few times; it might be worth adding a util method to dedup as well as make conditions differentiating spatial vs temporal methods clearer (like what's already happening with spatial_mode/temporal_mode later). Also imo it's confusing having `use_fsr` and `use_mfx` both be false when using the temporal versions of either but 🤷

yes, it has a similar aa effect to fsr2. Anecdotally looking at bistro with this branch I find the edges generally more naturally smoothed compared to fsr's characteristic oversharpened look but although they both exhibit some flickering fsr2 seems to stabilize in more situations than MetalFX temporal. Baseline, no aa FSR2 (default sharpening but this result was similar for many values) MetalFX Temporal When zoomed in, MetalFX temporal definitely loses some detail and edge definition but at native resolution I personally prefer it to the fake detail in fsr.

Per @clayjohn, these need to be included in the public APIs, so that they can be selected on a per-platform basis. Windows will have the option for a DirectX-specific scaler too. There may still be some details to work out here.

I'm not fully convinced we should be exposing this enum at the RenderingDevice level, as it'll fail to get documented. I think we might need to make an entirely new enumerator and map it to the driver one internally. This enum is entirely for the RenderingDeviceGraph, and we don't want to expose its information to clients of RenderingDevice.

CC @clayjohn would it be acceptable to create a new enum here instead?

Remember that different users working on the same project might be able to see those options, so if you couldn't, the scene would be saved with different values once you save it in the editor (since your inspector's enum would have fewer options available).

Therefore, the set of available properties in the inspector should remain the same across platforms.

Yeah I was thinking about removing this comment because definitely the simplest and least surprising thing would be to just list all options although FWIW setting this to an unsupported value causes it to fallback to not using scaling at runtime but it doesn't overwrite the project settings file even when other options are changed.

Maybe an option later on would be higher level cross platform options like `Off, Bilinear, Spatial, Temporal` with flags to allow those to defer to platform specific apis when available/appropriate, so if a project was using metal by default it would use fsr automatically rather than disabling scaling entirely on a non-mac. That might be too rigid for other scaling options to fit in, for example it looks like DirectSR does not make the distinction in the same way, but I imagine this will come up for other api specific additions in the future like frame gen.

I learned that compute shaders can't read / write to MSAA textures (at least not on Metal), so for now when enabling MetalFX temporal, it prints a warning and disables MSAA internally, similar to how FSR2 / MetalFX temporal disables TAA internally.
@DarioSamo I wonder if we should just move the entire `ResourceUsage` enum over from RDG to `RenderingDeviceCommons` , so that there is only one copy of it?
Final change was to introduce a new enum into `RenderingDevice` that has the same variants as `ResourceUsage` and statically asserts they are the same, so we can cast directly.

Is it possible some compiler could complain about this control path not returning anything even if it's supposed to crash?

While inefficient, it'd be perfectly possible for a user to run into problems with this limitation, as just making four viewports that use scaling (e.g. player split-screen) would easily cause it. There's a few alternate solutions that'd allow this to scale without running into this issue that might be hard to catch in the future.

One possibility is that it should be pretty safe to assume that an argument structure can be discarded and reused once the callback for it is called. A growing vector and a free list should make it easy to achieve this. Look for a free spot or expand the vector on creation, mark it as deleted and free from the vector when the callback is processed. Then your callback arguments can just be the index to this vector.
This will only get compiled on macOS, so it will be ok. I included it as a guard to indicate a programming error

Right, good catch! My assumption here is clearly wrong, as I was just assuming a max of triple buffering. 

❓Do we have existing examples or data structures for managing a free list or will I have to implement it myself?

No ready-made template as far as I know, but the logic is pretty straightforward. Just keep two vectors and use one to track the indices that are free (free list) and the other one to track the contents. Whenever you try to use an element, check if there's anything in the free list. If there is, pop the back. If not, expand the contents vector. On deletion, insert the index into the free list.

There should be some examples with semaphores and swap chains using a similar free list mechanism in RenderingDevice I believe.
Sounds good – I will sort that out.

body: Is this making some sort of assumption of the command buffer already being started? That sounds alright, but will the command buffer remain open or reopen itself after the scaler is finished for other commands that might come afterwards? My main concern is if it's flexible enough against the reorder that might occur.

The intention behind it is clear, I was wondering if we're guaranteed the compiler will never complain about it. Something like this does result in an error due to being a warning in other platforms. I think for the sake of guarding against a possible future build error if the compiler changes or against other types of analysis we should be returning in all control paths anyway, even if it's never meant to reach it.

As you're reusing a previously used structure, you'll want to clear the contents of the exposure ID in the else branch here to indicate it's an empty ID. Otherwise you might end up using a stale reference.

Bit of a nitpick, but I'm not sure these local-scope enums help readability too much even if it's the intention behind them. For following the code below I have to check what the original viewport scaling enums map to in this scope, and the declaration is also repeated elsewhere in the code with different options.

I feel like it'd be preferrable to use the viewport enums and the extra verbosity would be appreciated, as the current method requires more back and forth in following the logic.

In theory it should not be possible for an invalid scaling mode to reach these functions as it's validated on a higher-level method usually that reverts it to "NONE" if the conditions don't apply. See `RendererViewport::_configure_3d_render_buffers` for further details on this. You can invalidate the MetalFX option if Metal isn't enabled at that level instead and save yourself some trouble.

We don't want to rely on stack allocation ideally on paths that take a variable amount of resources. I'm aware some parts of the code still use `alloca`, but it becomes a bit of a hazard when the size is unknown. I recommend switching to thread_local LocalVectors instead.

body:
This is an implementation detail of Metal and the `MDCommandBuffer`, as command buffers can't create new encoders if one is already outstanding. This already happens when switching between blits, render or compute pipelines. I could change the `MDCommandBuffer` to expose a method called `execute_spatial_upscale` and then it would call `end` automatically as an internal detail, like it does when binding a pipeline:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/76128893e0c2b1d5db589bced648098831bb2d18/drivers/metal/metal_objects.mm#L87-L96

I could also create one for `execute_temporal_upscale`.

body: I think it's good as long as it's aware that it needs to restart the buffer afterwards in later calls, I was just unsure and wanted to double check.

Basically, if either of these methods returns true is because it had to turn the immutable resource into a mutable one, therefore it introduces a synchronization as it has to throw away all the assumptions it made about the resource not needing to be tracked.

This scheme is followed by every other method that affects a resource in such a way, and it's safe to assume a resource involved in a driver callback requires the tracking as you're specifying a particular usage anyway.

This is purely metadata for the graph to solve and sort operations properly.

Your current code is correct, it's just not correctly accounting for the fact that the tracker might not exist. Calling the bits of code I showed above before either one will fix that situation.
Ahh, I'll just remove the platform guard, as we already have the DEV_ASSERT 👍🏻
Done!
Done – using PagedAllocator with 16 elements, as that should be more than enough. It will allocate new pages of 16 elements if we do happen to go over.
Brilliant, thanks!
Would it be better to check the `CALLBACK_RESOURCE_USAGE_` flags, and only call `_(texture|buffer)_make_mutable` it if the callback intends to write to it?

That alone might not be true for textures, as different read usages can still require layout transitions. For example, going from shader read to copy source requires a layout transition and therefore a tracker. You could be using multiple callbacks in a case like this and the graph would not insert the appropriate transition in the middle if the texture didn't have its tracker yet.

It's much easier in this case to create the tracker, and it's safe to do so. The amount of resources that are likely to go through this type of code is very small.
Fix this and simplified the code considerably. I've left some notes of the changes.
